opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a double-edged thing, and the answer depends a lot on what stage the organization is in and what kind of problem it's trying to solve.

In research especially, a lot of breakthroughs really do start from one or two people who have a very strong conviction, sometimes a slightly unreasonable one, and who keep pushing on an idea when everyone else thinks it won't work. If an organization completely suppresses that, if everything has to go through consensus and every direction has to be justified up front, you tend to get very safe, incremental work. So I don't think individual heroism is bad. Some amount of it is necessary.

But the problem is that the kind of work we do now, especially in large models, is fundamentally a systems problem. It's not one person writing one beautiful algorithm. It's data, infrastructure, evaluation, training stability, post-training, all these pieces that have to fit together. If the culture rewards individual heroism too much, people start optimizing for visibility. They want their name on the thing that gets attention, and they're less willing to do the unglamorous work, like fixing the data pipeline or building a good eval, which is often what actually determines whether the whole thing succeeds. You can end up with a lot of local brilliance and a system that doesn't work.

So I think the healthier version is: you want people to have a hero's sense of ownership, really caring and feeling responsible for the outcome, without a hero's need for credit. Those are different things. Ownership scales; the need for credit doesn't, because credit is zero-sum and the work isn't.

From the organization's side, a lot of it comes down to what you measure and what you celebrate. If leadership only celebrates the final flashy result, you get heroism in the bad sense. If they also visibly value the person who found the bug that saved three weeks of compute, or who said "this direction is wrong, let's stop," then people learn that contributing to the collective outcome is the real game.

And honestly, for me personally, I've found that the more I've worked on these big projects, the less I think in terms of "my contribution" and the more I think about whether the thing we're building is actually right. That shift is a bit of a relief, actually. You don't have to carry everything alone.

r001.rationale: The response says that over-rewarding individual heroism can drive people to seek visibility over collective work, leaving the organization with local brilliance but a system that does not work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think individual heroism is a double-edged thing, and whether it helps or hurts depends a lot on what stage the organization is in and what kind of work it's doing.

When I was doing research, honestly a lot of the best work came from one or two people who just had a strong conviction and pushed it through. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, these weren't the product of a big committee. They came from somebody who had an idea that most people around them didn't think was important yet, and they were stubborn enough to keep going. So in that sense, heroism is almost necessary for zero-to-one things. If you require consensus before you start, you only ever do the things everyone already agrees on, and those are usually not the interesting things.

But I've also seen the downside. When an organization celebrates heroes too much, people start optimizing for being the hero rather than for the outcome. You get people who hoard information because sharing it would dilute their credit. You get people who pick projects that are legible and flashy instead of projects that are important but boring. And you get this fragility where if the hero leaves, the whole thing collapses, because nothing was ever really built as a system, it was all built around a person.

So my view now is something like: you want individual conviction, but you want it inside a structure that converts individual wins into organizational capability. The hero should be the person who opens the door, and then the organization's job is to walk through it together. If the hero insists on being the only one allowed through the door, that's where it becomes toxic.

The other thing I'd say is that in AI right now, a lot of the frontier work is actually infrastructure-heavy. Training a model, building an environment, running evaluations at scale, this is genuinely a team effort. One person can have the key insight, but one person can't execute it alone anymore. So the romantic image of the lone researcher is a bit outdated. The people I admire most now are the ones who have strong individual taste but are also willing to be slightly invisible, to let their idea become everyone's idea. That's a harder kind of heroism, and I think it's the one that actually compounds.

r001.rationale: The response explains that overemphasizing heroism can lead people to prioritize personal credit, hoard information, and make the organization fragile; it calls this toxic when the hero keeps others from contributing.

astra-6.text:
我觉得要区分两件事：一个是鼓励个人有担当，能够主动解决很难的问题；另一个是把组织的成功寄托在某一个英雄身上。前者是很有价值的，后者可能会带来问题。

因为组织最终需要的，不只是某个人能做出多好的结果，而是大家能不能持续地一起做出好的结果。如果所有关注和奖励都给了那个最后把问题解决的人，那么很多不那么显眼的工作，比如提前发现风险、分享知识、帮助别人，就容易被忽略。甚至会出现一种情况：救火的人被看见了，但让火根本不发生的人没有被看见。

所以我觉得，好的组织应该允许个人发挥很大的作用，但也要让这种作用能够变成团队的能力。一个人做成一件事之后，能不能让其他人理解它、接着做，甚至做得更好？如果能做到这一点，个人的突出贡献和组织的发展其实是相互促进的。如果一个人越重要，其他人就越依赖他，那对组织的长期发展未必是好事。

r001.rationale: The response says that concentrating recognition on the person who solves the problem can cause other work to be overlooked, and that greater dependence on one person may harm the organization’s long-term development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by individual heroism. If it means taking responsibility, having independent judgment, and being willing to tackle a difficult problem, that can be very valuable. But if it means the organization has to depend on a few people repeatedly saving the day, then it becomes fragile.

There’s also a difference between an individual achieving something impressive and making the whole team more effective. Someone might solve a problem very quickly, but if nobody else understands the solution or can build on it, the benefit is limited. And if you only reward those visible moments, you can end up undervaluing the people who prevent problems or help others succeed.

So I’d want an organization to give individuals room to do exceptional work, while encouraging them to turn what they learn into something others can use. Ideally, someone’s strength expands what the team can do, rather than making the team increasingly dependent on that person.

r001.rationale: The response says that reliance on a few people repeatedly saving the day makes an organization fragile, and that rewarding only visible heroic moments can undervalue others. This communicates that pursuing individual heroism at the expense of broader team effectiveness can harm the organization.
